title: Transfer: K Closest Points to the Origin
oneLiner: Keep the k points nearest (0, 0). Same capped heap as Top-K, but now you want the smallest keys, so the heap has to evict the largest.
keyTakeaway: Top-K with a heap works for any key you can compute, not just the values themselves. To keep the K SMALLEST keys, cap a MAX-heap at size K: its top is the worst point you are keeping, which is exactly the one to evict when a closer point arrives. Compare squared distances to stay in integers.
explanation:
This follows Top-K Elements with the requirement changed in two ways: you want the k closest points to the origin (the k smallest distances, not the k largest values), and the key is computed from each item rather than being the item. Given points as [x, y] pairs and k, return the k points with the smallest distance to (0, 0). To make the answer unique, a tie in distance goes to the smaller x, then the smaller y, and the result is listed in that same order (nearest first).

Distance is sqrt(x^2 + y^2), but sqrt never changes which of two distances is smaller, so compare x^2 + y^2 and stay in exact integers. The full key is the triple (x^2 + y^2, x, y): one point is closer than another when its triple is smaller.

In Top-K Elements you kept a MIN-heap of size k, because to keep the largest you must be able to throw away the smallest of your candidates. Here everything flips. To keep the k smallest keys you need to find the LARGEST key among your candidates, so use a MAX-heap capped at k: push each point, and whenever the heap holds more than k, pop its top (the farthest, with ties going to the larger x and y). At the end the heap holds the k closest; sort them by key for the answer.

In C#, PriorityQueue is a min-heap, so give it a comparer that reverses the order of the key, or negate the key. In Python, heapq is a min-heap too: push (-d, -x, -y) so the farthest point is on top. Each of the n points costs O(log k), so O(n log k) time and O(k) space, against O(n log n) for sorting all of them.

The visualization runs points [3, 3], [5, -1], [-2, 4], [1, 1] with k = 2. The cells are the heap's contents as (squared distance) point.

Explain why the same idea works: before you move on, write two or three sentences on why Top-K Elements needed a MIN-heap but this needs a MAX-heap, even though both keep "the best k". What does the top of the heap have to be in each case, and why is that the only element you ever need to look at?

recognitionSignals: The k nearest, cheapest, smallest or most similar items by some computed score.
A stream or large input where you only need to remember k items at a time.
gotchas: To keep the k SMALLEST keys, evict the largest: a max-heap. A min-heap here throws away the closest points.
Compare x * x + y * y, not the square root: integers compare exactly and the order is the same.
Ties: the key must include x and y, or which of two equally distant points survives depends on heap order.
confusableWith: Top-K Elements: Use a Heap is the same capped heap for the k largest values, which needs the opposite (min) heap.

complexity.note: Each of n points does one push and at most one pop on a heap capped at k + 1 items, O(log k) each; the final sort of k points is O(k log k), which is no more. Sorting every point instead costs O(n log n).
